en: The Pācittiya Section of the Mahāvibhaṅga of the Theravāda Vinaya
The Chapter on Exhortation 25.
The Training Rule on the Giving of Robes.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was walking for alms in a certain street in Sāvatthī, and a certain bhikkhunī was also walking for alms in that same street.
Then that bhikkhu said this to the bhikkhunī: “Go, sister; alms are being given in such-and-such a place.
She also said this: “Go, venerable sir; alms are being given in such-and-such a place.”
They became visible to her through constant sight.
Now at that time, the robe-cloth of the Saṅgha was being distributed.
Then that bhikkhunī, having gone for the exhortation, approached that bhikkhu; having approached and paid homage to him, she stood to one side.
As that bhikkhunī was standing to one side, the bhikkhu said to her: “Sister, this is my share of robe-cloth; will you accept it?
“Yes, venerable sir, for I have poor-quality robes.
Then the bhikkhu gave the robe-cloth to that bhikkhunī.
That monk, too, had fragile robes.
The monks said to that monk, “Friend, now you must make up your robe.
Then that monk reported this matter to the monks.
Those monks who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can a monk give a robe to a nun? ... [and so on] ...
"Is it true, monk, that you gave a robe to a nun?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
“Are your relatives, monk, unrelated to you?
“They are unrelated, Blessed One.”
“An unrelated person, foolish man, does not know whether [an action] is appropriate or inappropriate, or whether it is proper or improper.
How can you, foolish man, give a robe to an unrelated bhikkhunī?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].”
And so, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whichever monk should give a robe to an unrelated nun, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not give robes in exchange for those of the bhikkhunīs.
The bhikkhunīs complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can it be that the venerable ones will not give us robes in exchange?"
The monks heard those nuns grumbling, complaining, and expressing their indignation.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, to give a trade-exchange to five [persons]:
to a monk, to a nun, to a female trainee, to a male novice,
and to a female novice— I allow you, monks, to give a trade-exchange to these five.”
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"Whosoever, however, a monk should give a robe to an unrelated nun, except in exchange, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
"Whosoever, however" means:
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"Non-relative" means one who is not connected by blood on the mother's side or the father's side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors.
"Bhikkhunī" means...
One who is fully ordained in both Saṅghas.
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes that is suitable for assignment and is of the last [permissible] type.
"Except in exchange": if one gives a robe setting aside the exchange, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one gives a robe to a woman who is not a relative, perceiving her as not being a relative, except in exchange, there is an offense of expiation.
If he gives a robe to one who is not related while being in doubt, except in exchange, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he gives a robe to one who is not related while perceiving her as a relative, except in exchange, there is an offense of expiation.
If he gives a robe to one ordained on one side (a female), except in exchange, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is a relative, but he perceives her as not being a relative, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is a relative, but he is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is a relative, and he perceives her as a relative, there is no offense.
There is no offense:
if it is for a relative;
or if there is an exchange, such as small for large, or large for small.
A bhikkhunī accepts it on trust,
she accepts it for a limited time,
or she gives another requisite, excluding a robe.
for one undergoing training,
for a female novice,
for one who is insane,
"For one who is a first offender.
The fifth training rule on the giving of robes is concluded.
